Orla Minihane’s Restore Exit Puts Party Culture Under Scrutiny

The former women’s safety spokeswoman says she was targeted after speaking up for victims from different backgrounds. Rupert Lowe rejects the wider criticism of his party.

By Steve English · 1 November 2026

Orla Minihane’s account of leaving Restore Britain has put the party’s internal culture under fresh scrutiny. In a new interview with The Telegraph, the former spokeswoman for women’s safety describes a breakdown in her relationship with the party after she argued that women and girls from every background must be included in safeguarding work.

The dispute came into focus after a Restore event in Gateshead in July. Minihane says she spoke about female genital mutilation and the need to protect non-white girls born in Britain, alongside her work on crimes against women by migrant men. She says her comments were selectively clipped and circulated online, triggering what she described as an all-out attack on her character. The Telegraph’s account reports her claim that people in the party’s operation then cut her off and that Lowe stopped reaching out.

Minihane’s criticism is directed chiefly at the people she says run Restore day to day. She described them as “power-mad” and “deeply abusive”, and argued that Lowe was not properly in control of the operation. She said he was not a bad or evil man, but warned that unless he addressed those around him, the party could lose support. These are her allegations and assessment of the organisation.

Earlier claims of abuse

Her latest account follows a report published in September, when she left Restore after about seven months as a member. The Telegraph reported that she said she had been called “mudblood” at a party meeting because she is half Irish, and that someone at another meeting asked whether she would save an Indian girl who was drowning. The report also carried accounts from unnamed Restore figures who alleged racism, antisemitism, misogyny and threats within the party. AOL republishes that Telegraph report.

In a separate interview after she resigned as spokeswoman, Minihane also described abuse aimed at her and her family after she spoke up for non-white victims. Searchlight reported her account, including her allegation that the abuse extended to attacks on her daughter and threats involving her nieces.

Lowe’s response

Rupert Lowe said he respected Minihane’s work on women’s safety and had spoken with her regularly. In response to the latest report, he rejected its wider portrayal of Restore, describing it as another attempt to smear the party. His response is included in The Telegraph article.

Minihane has now returned to Reform UK. Her account raises a direct question for Restore’s leadership: how will it respond to claims that members and people close to the party’s operation abused a senior spokeswoman after she challenged the way women’s safety was being discussed?
